Bars private citizens from corresponding with a foreign government, without authority, in order to influence its conduct in a dispute with the United States or to defeat U.S. measures.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 1 Stat. 613](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/1/613){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 18 U.S.C. 953](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/953?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Applies to any U.S. citizen acting without the authority of the United States.
- Covers correspondence or intercourse with a foreign government or its agents.
- Requires intent to influence that government's conduct in a dispute with the United States, or to defeat U.S. measures.

## Why it matters

It is cited far more often than it is used, usually as a political charge against unofficial diplomacy. It expresses the principle that the government speaks with one voice abroad, and it is the diplomatic counterpart of the [Neutrality Act](neutrality-1794.qmd). Modern concerns about foreign influence are handled through [FARA](fara-1938.qmd) instead.

## Current status

In force. There have been two indictments, in 1803 and 1852, and no convictions.

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}
